title: Rooftop Farming Returns to the City

passages.title: Rooftop Farming Returns to the City

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early twentieth century, many European cities kept small vegetable plots on flat roofs, but the practice faded after cheap refrigerated transport made it easier to bring produce from distant farms. By the 1970s, rooftops were seen mainly as places for water tanks and ventilation equipment.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Interest returned in the 2000s, driven less by food security than by concerns about heat. Dark roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release it at night, raising neighbourhood temperatures. Researchers in Montreal recorded surface temperatures on a planted roof that were up to 30 degrees Celsius lower than on a nearby bitumen roof during a summer afternoon.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The weight of soil remains the main engineering obstacle. Saturated soil can be extremely heavy, so most commercial rooftop farms now use lightweight growing media made from expanded clay or recycled materials. Some operators avoid soil entirely and rely on hydroponic systems, in which plant roots sit in nutrient-rich water.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Economic results are mixed. A farm in Brooklyn that opened in 2010 reported that restaurant contracts, rather than sales at local markets, provided most of its income in its first five years. However, a survey of 42 rooftop projects in North America found that fewer than a third covered their operating costs from food sales alone; many relied on educational programmes or corporate events.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: City governments have begun to respond. Several have changed building regulations so that a roof garden no longer counts towards a building's height limit, and a few offer tax reductions to owners who install vegetation. Critics argue that such incentives mainly benefit wealthy developers, yet supporters point out that cooler streets help all residents, especially elderly people during heatwaves.
